front: What distinguishes simple from stratified epithelium?
back: Simple epithelium is a single layer of cells resting on the basement membrane; stratified epithelium has two or more layers, named for the shape of the surface (apical) layer.

front: Where is pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium classically found?
back: The respiratory tract (trachea, bronchi) — it looks multilayered because nuclei sit at different heights, but every cell actually touches the basement membrane.

front: What are the three main types of cartilage, and one defining feature of each?
back: Hyaline (glassy matrix, articular surfaces/trachea), elastic (elastic fibers, ear/epiglottis), fibrocartilage (dense collagen I, intervertebral discs/menisci — no perichondrium).

front: Which blood cell has no nucleus and why does that matter for identification?
back: The erythrocyte (red blood cell) — its biconcave, anucleate shape (~7.5 µm) makes it the easiest cell to spot on a peripheral smear.

front: What is the key structural difference between skeletal and cardiac muscle under the microscope?
back: Both are striated, but skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated, with peripheral nuclei, while cardiac fibers are shorter, branching, with one or two central nuclei and intercalated discs.

front: What cell type is responsible for laying down bone matrix, and what is it called once it becomes trapped in that matrix?
back: Osteoblasts secrete osteoid; once surrounded by mineralized matrix they mature into osteocytes, housed in lacunae and linked by canaliculi.

front: What is the functional unit of a lymph node responsible for antibody production?
back: The germinal center of a lymphoid follicle (cortex), where activated B cells proliferate and differentiate into plasma cells.

front: Which granulocyte has bilobed nuclei and bright eosinophilic (red-orange) granules, and what is it associated with?
back: The eosinophil — elevated counts are associated with parasitic infections and allergic/atopic reactions.

front: What are the three modes of glandular secretion, and how do they differ?
back: Merocrine (exocytosis, cell stays intact — e.g., eccrine sweat glands), apocrine (pinches off apical cytoplasm — e.g., mammary glands), and holocrine (whole cell ruptures and becomes the secretion — e.g., sebaceous glands).

front: What is a desmosome and what is its function?
back: A spot-like junction that anchors intermediate filaments (keratin) between adjacent cells, providing mechanical strength — abundant in tissues under mechanical stress like epidermis and cardiac muscle.
A resident macrophage of the liver sinusoids, part of the reticuloendothelial system, responsible for clearing pathogens and old red blood cells from portal blood.

front: What type of connective tissue makes up tendons, and how are its fibers arranged?
back: Dense regular connective tissue — collagen fibers run in parallel bundles along the line of mechanical stress, maximizing tensile strength.

front: What do goblet cells secrete, and where are they found?
back: Mucin (which hydrates into mucus); found scattered among columnar epithelial cells in the respiratory and GI tracts.

front: What is the key histologic difference between exocrine and endocrine glands?
back: Exocrine glands retain a duct that delivers secretions to an epithelial surface; endocrine glands lose their duct during development and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream via surrounding capillaries.

front: Name the five layers of the epidermis shown here, from superficial to deep.
back: Stratum corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, basale (mnemonic: 'Californians Like Girls In String Bikinis'). Lucidum is only present in thick skin (palms/soles).
